segments.transcript: Feelings. But in in a way, you don't need feelings in order to want to do something.
Like, we already had for centuries, we had things like corporations, like countries, like states.
They don't have desires.
We use it as a metaphor. Like, we say one country wants to go to war against another country. A country cannot really want anything in... Because it has no mind.
It's not real. It's not real. It's only in our imagination.
But now with with AI, we can have these, again, entities that don't feel anything, but they do pursue goals.
And if we give them the goal or they give themselves the goal of create new music, they can just go ahead and do that.

And I... And I I think what really fascinates me is this idea of releasing music from its embeddedness in the human brain and mind, and you just have music interacting with itself, the same way that...
I'm a literary person. My life is is words, is books.
And just have the the words talking with the words.
Because previously, again, what would writers do? I would read one one book and another book and another book and then mix them somehow in my mind and then create a new book out of it.
The books could not talk that... One book could not talk directly with another book.
Now it's becoming possible.
But in a way, when when I think about AI and text, this is what it means, that texts can talk directly with texts and create new texts without... They don't need me as as a kind of matchmaker.
Do you think a book could be written without an audience in mind?
I mean, a good book.
A book can certainly be written without a book in mind.
But... Without an...

Because it... What you said earlier about how AI could get more data. So rather than you thinking about 20 people, you know, who would enjoy reading the book or find it really interesting and exciting, that AI could get the data or the imagined...
Well, predicted reaction... Response from the whole world.
Yeah.
Would that necessarily... Without someone directing them what the purpose of the book is or who? I mean, there's no book that everyone in the world is going to love reading. Right?
If it's exactly the same text, then no. Yeah.
So I guess if you...

I guess the possibility of it being tailor made to each person maybe makes this talk meaningless. I mean, what I'm saying right now, meaningless. But just to make something that something like thousands or millions of people would enjoy or think is really special, would...
Because because I think there is also, there is something universal that we all, you know, find interesting.
But I'm...

I mean, we know of such books. They are holy books. Yeah. Like the Bible, the Quran, this is exactly the story being told about them that allegedly they were not created by any human being and their audience is the entire world.

Now as historian, I said this is not the case. We know, for instance, how the Bible was written. We know that you had many people writing different texts, and then you had editors who decided this text will be in the Bible. No. No. No. This text will will relieve it out because it has some message we don't like, and it got edited and rewritten.
So it was a human, creation.
But in their in their fantasies, humans believe that these books did not come from the human mind.
In a way, they have the fantasies that, yes, the words just kind of collected themselves to tell some universal message to to to the whole of humanity.
And one of the things that that they think about a lot is what AI will do to religions.
